what_it_does: AI chips do most of their work multiplying pairs of numbers together and adding them up millions of times per second; one way to speed this up is to notice that many of those numbers are zero and simply skip the multiplication. This paper looks at a technique called 'bit-slice' processing, where each number is cut into small chunks of bits (the binary digits that computers use) and only the non-zero chunks are sent forward for computation. Prior designs could skip zeros in either the input data or the stored model weights, but not both at the same time and not at this fine-grained chunk level; the proposed chip design called BADA does both simultaneously. The authors also add a training-time trick that nudges the weight numbers toward zero in their upper bits, creating more zero chunks to skip. The abstract suggests meaningful efficiency gains, but exact numbers would need to be verified from the full paper.
